# LiFePO4 vs NMC: LiFePO4 is the better buy for most people

Most of the sources agree that LiFePO4 (LFP) is the better choice for most buyers ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/), [OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/), [PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/learn/lifepo4-vs-nmc)).

| | LiFePO4 | NMC |
|---|---|---|
| **Cycle life** | Typically 2,000-6,000 cycles | Typically 500-2,000 cycles |
| **Safety in failure** | Burns cooler and slower | Hotter and more violent |
| **Weight** | Slightly heavier per Wh | Lighter at the cell level |
| **Price per Wh** | Median about $0.55 | Median about $0.95 |

- **Cycle life:** This is the biggest difference. Charged and drained daily, a 500-cycle NMC unit lasts about 1.4 years, and a 3,000-cycle LFP unit about 8 years. The figures come from [UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/).
- **Safety:** In lab tests, LFP cells peaked at much lower temperatures than NMC cells when they failed ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). LFP is not fireproof, though. One test found LFP reached thermal runaway sooner under overcharge, so a good battery management system matters either way ([UnpluggedWatts](https://www.unpluggedwatts.com/lifepo4-vs-nmc-power-station/)).
- **Weight:** NMC cells hold more energy per kilogram, but the gap mostly shrinks in finished products. Across one database, the median NMC station held only about 10% more Wh per pound ([OutageMath](https://www.outagemath.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc/)). Another site found a 16% gap ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)). Compare actual model specs rather than assuming the chemistry decides.
- **Cold weather:** Chemistry matters less than you might expect. Most stations of either type refuse to charge below 32°F, so check the manual for your model ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)).

## When NMC still makes sense
- You need the lightest possible unit and will use it rarely.
- You find a deeply discounted unit for occasional use, such as a few weekends a year or rare outages. Cycle life barely matters there.
- You already own a working NMC unit. There's no need to replace it.

## Buying tips
- **Check the cycle rating's end point.** "3,000 cycles to 80%" is a stronger promise than "4,000 to 70%." Brands also test under different conditions.
- **Confirm the chemistry on the spec sheet.** Some pages don't state it.
- **Look at the warranty.** Warranties range from 2 to 5 years, and a warranty is a promise you can actually claim on ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/lifepo4-vs-nmc)).
